Foraging for wild edibles isÂ a viable optionÂ when you’ve run out of food while bugging out. The wildernessÂ has an abundance of edible plants that canÂ be eaten inÂ emergency situations. However,Â you can’t just eat anything you find growing in the wild because some plants are poisonous. (h/t toPreppersWill.com)

Here’s a nine-step universal edibility test to help youÂ identifyÂ wild edibles.

You need to look for a plant that grows abundantly in the area because this edibility test will take some time. If you pick a rare plant, you will have to searchÂ for more of it orÂ waste your efforts should it turn out to be poisonous.

Once you find the plant you want to test, look for a sample and pick it while wearing hand gloves. This will protect your skin in case the plant is toxic. Make sure that your sampleÂ grows a distance away from other plant species in the area.Â Picking a sample that has come in contact with other plants can compromise your test.

You also need to separate the different parts of the plant,Â such as the flowers, stem, leaves, buds, seeds and roots,Â because some parts may be edible while others are poisonous.

Throw away parts of the plant that smell unpleasant.

Gently pressÂ each of the remaining plant parts onto your elbows and wrists for about 15 minutes. If the concerned area feels numb, itchy or hot or if you observe rashes beginning to form, remove the plant material right away and get rid of it.

Make sure to use a differentÂ area of yourÂ skin for every plant part to maintain the integrity of the edibility test.

It’s still unclear at this point ifÂ the remaining plant parts areÂ actually edible. But boiling them can eliminate the germs or toxins that may be present.

Boil each remaining plant part separatelyÂ to avoid cross-contamination of the good parts with the bad parts. Rinse the parts thoroughly after boiling.

If you’re doing the edibility test while in the wild,start a fireusing materials around you.Â You can find manyÂ tree branches, dried leaves and other natural fuels in the wild. You can also check your bug-out bag for a steel container that you can place over the fire.

Press a small amount of each plant part on a smallÂ area of yourÂ upper or lower lipÂ and hold for a few minutes.Â If you experience any of the adverse reactions described above, discard the plant part. Make sure to use only a smallÂ area of your lip so you can test the remaining parts without comprising the test.

Move onto the next step if there is no adverse reactionÂ after 15 minutes.

Take a small bite of the plant part andÂ place it on your tongue. If there’s no adverse reaction, chew andhold it in your mouth for 15 minutes. Do not swallow.

If no burning, itching, numbing, stinging or other irritation occurs, swallow it. Wait for several hours to see if you experience an adverse reaction, such as nausea, vomiting anddiarrhea. If any of this happens, induce vomiting and drink a lot of water to flush out the toxins.

If all is well, proceed to the last step.

Take a bigger morsel than the test piece and swallow it without chewing. Wait for a few hours. If you don’t feel anything strange, the plant part should be safe for eating. (Related:ÂEverything you need to know aboutÂ foragingÂ for food when SHTF.)

This edibility test is intended only for green leafy plants and not for fungi, moss and the like.Â It’s also recommended thatÂ youÂ pack enough food to avoid the needÂ toÂforage while bugging out. While foraging has its uses, eating foods straight from your bug-out bag saves youÂ time and effort.
